title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: At midday on October twenty-second, Pierre was trudging uphill along the muddy, slippery road, looking at his feet and at the roughness of the way. Occasionally he glanced at the familiar crowd around him, then back at his feet again. Both were equally familiar and felt like part of himself. The blue-gray, bandy-legged dog ran merrily alongside the road, sometimes lifting one hind leg to hop along on three as proof of its agility and good spirits, then going on all four again and rushing off to bark at crows sitting on carrion. The dog was merrier and sleeker than it had been in Moscow. All around lay the flesh of different creatures—from humans to horses—in various stages of decay; and since wolves were kept away by the passing men, the dog could eat all it wanted.

It had been raining since morning, seeming as though it might stop any minute and the sky clear, but after a brief pause it rained harder than before. The saturated road no longer absorbed the water, which ran along the ruts in streams.
Pierre walked along looking from side to side, counting his steps in threes and ticking them off on his fingers. Mentally addressing the rain, he repeated: "Come on now, come on! Pour harder!"

He seemed to be thinking of nothing, but deep down inside him, his soul was occupied with something important and comforting. This something was a very subtle spiritual insight drawn from a conversation with Karataev the day before.

At their previous stopping place, feeling chilled by a dying campfire, Pierre had gotten up and gone to the next one, which was burning better. There Platon Karataev sat covered up—head and all—with his greatcoat as if it were a vestment, telling the soldiers in his warm and pleasant, though now weakened voice, a story Pierre already knew. It was past midnight, the hour when Karataev was usually free of his fever and especially lively. When Pierre reached the fire and heard Platon's voice, weakened by illness, and saw his thin face brightly lit by the blaze, he felt a painful stab in his heart. His feeling of pity for this man frightened him, and he wanted to leave, but there was no other fire, so Pierre sat down, trying not to look at Platon.
"How am I? If we complain about sickness, God won't grant us death," replied Platon, and immediately resumed the story he had begun.
"And so, brother," he continued, with a smile on his pale, wasted face and a particularly joyful light in his eyes, "you see, brother..."

Pierre had long been familiar with that story. Karataev had told it to him alone some half-dozen times, always with a special joyful emotion. But though he knew it well, Pierre now listened as though it were something new, and the quiet rapture Karataev clearly felt as he told it communicated itself to Pierre as well. The story was about an old merchant who lived a good and God-fearing life with his family, and who once went to the Nizhni fair with a companion—a rich merchant.

Having checked into an inn, they both went to sleep, and the next morning the companion was found robbed and with his throat cut. A blood-stained knife was found under the old merchant's pillow. He was tried, flogged, and his nostrils torn off, "all in proper form" as Karataev put it, and he was sent to hard labor in Siberia.

"And so, brother" (it was at this point that Pierre had come up), "ten years or more passed. The old man was living as a convict, accepting his lot as he should and doing no wrong. He only prayed to God for death. Well, one night the convicts were gathered together just as we are, with the old man among them. And they began telling what each was being punished for and how they had sinned against God. One told how he had taken a life, another had taken two, a third had set a house on fire, while another had simply been a vagrant and done nothing wrong. So they asked the old man: 'What are you being punished for, old father?' 'I, my dear brothers,' said he, 'am being punished for my own and other men's sins. But I have not killed anyone or taken anything that was not mine—I have only helped my poorer brothers. I was a merchant, dear brothers, and had much property.' And he went on to tell them everything in proper order. 'I don't grieve for myself,' he says, 'God, it seems, has chosen to punish me. Only I am sorry for my old wife and the children,' and the old man began to weep. Now it happened that in the group was the very man who had killed the other merchant. 'Where did it happen, old father?' he said. 'When, and in what month?' He asked about everything, and his heart began to ache. So he came up to the old man like this, and fell down at his feet! 'You are suffering because of me, old father,' he says. 'It's the absolute truth, lads, that this man,' he says, 'is being tortured innocently and for nothing! I,' he says, 'did that deed, and I slipped the knife under your head while you were asleep. Forgive me, old father,' he says, 'for Christ's sake!'"
Karataev paused, smiling joyfully as he gazed into the fire, and pushed the logs together.

"And the old man said, 'God will forgive you—we are all sinners in His sight. I suffer for my own sins,' and he wept bitter tears. Well, and what do you think, dear friends?" Karataev continued, his face brightening more and more with a radiant smile, as if what he was about to say contained the chief beauty and the whole meaning of his story: "What do you think, dear fellows? That murderer confessed to the authorities. 'I have taken six lives,' he says (he was a great sinner), 'but what I am most sorry for is this old man. Don't let him suffer because of me.' So he confessed, and it was all written down, and the papers were sent off in proper form. The place was far away, and while they were processing things, what with one thing and another, filling in all the papers in proper form—the authorities, I mean—time passed. The case reached the Tsar. Eventually the Tsar's decree came: to set the merchant free and give him the compensation that had been awarded. The paper arrived and they began looking for the old man. 'Where is the old man who has been suffering innocently?' A paper has come from the Tsar!' So they began looking for him," here Karataev's lower jaw trembled, "but God had already forgiven him—he was dead! That's how it was, dear fellows!" Karataev concluded, and sat for a long time in silence, gazing before him with a smile.

And Pierre's soul was dimly but joyfully filled—not by the story itself, but by its mysterious meaning: by the radiant joy that lit up Karataev's face as he told it, and by the profound significance of that joy.
